catalog_quote: [p.56] Although Alaaba cannot be called a tone language, tone accent plays a crucial role, not least so for the case system. (If a word carries accent on a non-final syllable, the last vowel is devoiced, marked here by brackets.) [p.57, 2.1 Absolutive] Masculine nouns are characterized by different word-final vowels: high-pitched á, í, or ú, áa, ée and óo. ... Formally, the members of this semantic group are not a special sub-group, but they are found in any of the noun groups ending with short but pitch-bearing vowels. Feminine nouns, as they appear in citation, almost all have the ending -t(a), accent lies on the penultima. The vowel before -t(a) can be á, í, or ú, áa or ée; in addition, some few words end in short é or ó (no -t(a) suffixed). [p.61, 2.2 Nominative] The accent of masculine nouns is shifted to the left, the last vowel is devoiced (u) for words having in citation form short vowels word-finally, and long óo otherwise (the only exception is wúu 'water, NOM'). Feminine and plural nouns end in -t(i), the accent remains on the penultima. Feminine nouns ending with é in their citation form have the Nominative ending (i) and those ending with ó have (u) word-finally, the brackets indicating that the accent is on a non-final syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Alaaba has one culminative 'tone accent' (high pitch) per word whose position is fixed by morphology, not by a phonological count: in the citation form (Absolutive) masculine nouns carry the accent on the word-final vowel, feminine nouns in -t(a) on the penult; the Nominative is formed by shifting the accent one syllable leftward (masculine) while -t(i) feminines/plurals keep penult accent; whenever the accent is non-final the final vowel is devoiced. Net effect: accent sits in a final/penult window on nouns, chosen by gender class and case. Crass 2005 (Aethiopica 8: 295, first-hand, also saved) states the same architecture for the K'abeena variety: 'stress accent' with an unmarked position per word class - final for one group of nouns and verbal nouns, penultimate for the other nouns and adverbs - and nominative marked by accent shift to the preceding syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the pages read. Clause level (p.78): 'usually the main accent lies on the inflected verb'; the verb of a relative clause carries no accent and the first accent falls on the head noun.
new_statements.exceptions: p.61: wúu 'water, NOM' is the only exception to the masculine nominative pattern (short-vowel nouns take devoiced (u), long-vowel nouns óo); p.57: 'some few' feminine nouns end in short é or ó without -t(a). For K'abeena, Crass 2005 p.31 (snippet): in the nominative the accent moves to the antepenult when the accusative-accented vowel is short; no shift when the final vowel is long.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern nouns in citation form (= Absolutive) and case-inflected forms; accent is grammatical (case/gender), realised as high pitch; the grammar (2007: 10, via Sava's review) frames final-vowel devoicing within the '(phrasal) word which has a high pitch on a non-final syllable'. The chapter is a morphosyntax chapter by the author of the 2007 reference grammar, whose dedicated sec. 2.7 'Prosodic Features' (pp.42-47) was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog alab1254 'Alaba-K'abeena' (ISO alw) unites two separately described varieties: Alaaba/Halaba (Schneider-Blum 2007, 2009; fieldwork in Alaaba Kuliito) and K'abeena/Qabeena (Crass 2005; Wolkite area, K'abeena special woreda). The quoted statement is for Alaaba; Crass's first-hand abstract (Aethiopica 8: 295-296, saved) gives the parallel statement for K'abeena (stress accent, unmarked final or penultimate position by word class, nominative = accent shift leftward). Schneider-Blum (2009: 56) treats Alaaba as a language distinct from Kambaata (kamb1316).

new_statements.relation_note: Describes K'abeena, the sister variety of Alaaba under the same Glottolog code alab1254 ('Alaba-K'abeena'), not Alaaba proper. Placement is compatible with the existing Alaaba statement (Schneider-Blum 2009: final high-pitched vowel on masculine nouns, penult on feminine -t(a) nouns, leftward shift in the nominative with devoicing of the final vowel): Crass gives the same ultima/penult split by noun class and the same leftward nominative shift. It differs in type label: Crass treats it as a stress (Druck-)accent, whereas Schneider-Blum 2009 calls Alaaba prominence a 'tone accent' and says Alaaba 'cannot be called a tone language'. Only snippets of pp.30-33 and 86-88 were read, not the full…
new_statements.rule_in_words: K'abeena has a stress accent (Crass calls HEC 'stress accent languages', p.30) that falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable. Which one is a property of the word's inflection class: group-A nouns (and verbal nouns) are stressed on the ultima, group-B nouns (and adverbs) on the penult; a word whose accent is not final has a whispered (devoiced) final vowel. Case morphology moves the accent: the nominative is marked by shifting the accent one syllable to the left (ultima to penult in group A, to the antepenult in group B, p.31/87) when the class vowel is short; secondary cases carry the accent on their long suffix vowel (p.86, p.88). Verb forms also differ by accent (converb 1 final vs 2SG imperative penult, p.33).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned in the snippets seen
new_statements.exceptions: Nominative accent shift does not apply when the accusative final vowel is long (p.31); inflection classes 7 and 8 behave differently (p.87); secondary case suffixes with a long vowel always carry the accent (p.86, p.88); accent is marked explicitly only where it deviates from the two default rules (p.30).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog alab1254 is 'Alaba-K'abeena'. Work 0 (Schneider-Blum 2007) describes Alaaba; work 1 (Crass 2005) describes K'abeena (Qebena), the other variety under the same code, whose accent system Crass describes in the same terms (ultima vs penult by noun class, leftward nominative shift). The existing catalog statement is from Schneider-Blum 2009 on Alaaba.

In the unmarked position the accent lies on the last (ultima) or the second-to-last syllable (penult). If the accent is not on the ultima, the final vowel is whispered. [...] If the final vowel is not written superscript, the accent is on the ultima unless the accent is marked explicitly. 2. new_statements.relation_note: Describes K'abeena (the sister variety under the same Glottolog code alab1254), not Alaaba proper. Placement pattern is the same as the catalog record from Schneider-Blum 2009 for Alaaba (final accent in one noun group, penult in the other, leftward shift in the nominative with devoicing of the final vowel), so it is compatible and adds the K'abeena detail (inflection-class conditioning, antepenult in nominative of penult-accented nouns, suffix-accented secondary cases). Type label differs: Crass calls it a stress accent ('Druckakzentsystem', p.30, following Appleyard 1991), Schneider-Blum 2009 calls Alaaba prominence 'tone accent'. Statement already held by the project from the same snippe…
new_statements.rule_in_words: K'abeena has a stress accent (Druckakzent) whose unmarked position is the final or the penultimate syllable depending on the word's lexical group (group A nouns final, group B nouns penult; accent sits on the inflection-class vowel); a non-final accent devoices (whispers) the word-final vowel; the nominative is marked by shifting the accent one syllable leftward (ultima -> penult, penult -> antepenult) when the inflection-class vowel is short; secondary cases carry the accent on the long vowel of the case suffix (p.86, p.88); verbs: converb 1 final accent, 2sg imperative penult (p.33).
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the snippets read
new_statements.exceptions: no nominative accent shift when the accusative final vowel is long (p.31); inflection classes 7 and 8 behave differently in vowel-quality change (p.87); secondary cases always accented on the suffix long vowel (p.86)
new_statements.identity_note: Work 0 (Crass 2005) describes K'abeena (Wolkite area), the sister variety grouped with Alaaba under Glottolog alab1254 'Alaba-K'abeena'; work 1 (Schneider-Blum 2007) and the catalog record (Schneider-Blum 2009) describe Alaaba proper (Alaba special woreda, SNNPR).

readall_conflicts: The standing difference on record remains one of type label, not placement: Crass 2005 (K'abeena, snippets pp.30-33, 86-88) describes a stress accent (Druckakzent) on the ultima or penult by lexical noun group with a leftward shift in the nominative and whispering of the final vowel under non-final accent; Schneider-Blum 2009 (the catalog source, Alaaba proper) describes the same placement pattern but calls it 'tone accent' and says Alaaba 'cannot be called a tone language'. Schneider-Blum 2007 (sec. 2.7 'Prosodic Features') could not be opened, so its own wording is unverified.

sources.note: p.4 (second-hand): 'K'abeena has stress on the ultimate or penultimate syllable depending on the status of the final vowel (whispered or fully voiced; Crass 2005). Alaaba has word-level stress: feminine nouns have prominence on the penultimate syllable before t(a), while masculine and some feminine nouns have prominence on the final short vowel in the absolutive but on the penultimate syllable in the nominative with a final voiceless vowel (Schneider-Blum 2007).' Classes both among Cushitic 'stress languages'.
